stances.claim: The drug-trafficking case against the Espinosa Group collapsed because the police and prosecutors built it on Adorco's affidavits, which were inadmissible after the court denied his discharge as state witness, were taken without counsel of choice, violated his right against self-incrimination, and were recanted.
It is 'difficult, if not unfair' to fault the RTC for the shortcomings of the police and prosecution -- the court's hands were tied by the constitutional infirmities of the evidence.
stances.rhetorical_move: exonerating the judiciary from the political backlash

stances.claim: DOJ Secretary Guevarra has the authority and the gravitas to discipline the erring policemen and prosecutors and pursue remaining appellate remedies (RTC motion for reconsideration, then certiorari to the CA or SC).
Public confidence in the democratic process must be restored -- otherwise the failure tempts the citizenry toward authoritarian shortcuts and 'shoot first and ask questions later' mercenaries.

one_paragraph_summary: Panganiban diagnoses the Makati RTC's outright dismissal of the drug-trafficking charges against Kerwin Espinosa and three co-accused (Wu Tuan Yuan, Lovely Imperial, and Marcelo Adorco) as an 'embarrassing knockout' caused not by the court but by the lackadaisical and inept police and prosecution. The case stood on the affidavits and testimony of Adorco, whom prosecutors tried to convert into a state witness in October 2018 -- a motion the RTC denied on December 10, 2020. Without that discharge, Adorco's affidavits and statements (taken by PO3 Norman Abellanosa, SPO3 Benjamin Lamiseria, SPO2 Roberto Conol, and used by P/Supt. Richard Vercels alongside 'newspaper publications from the internet') were inadmissible -- they had been extracted without counsel of choice and in violation of the right against self-incrimination. Adorco then recanted via a 'Kontra Salaysay' on August 11, 2020. The RTC granted demurrers to the evidence, observing that without Adorco's testimony the prosecution's case 'necessarily crumbles.' Panganiban echoes the Inquirer editorial ('Grossly bungled case'): the ignominious collapse will define the twilight months of the drug war. But he refuses to scapegoat the court -- 'it is difficult, if not unfair, to fault the RTC for the shortcomings of the police and prosecution' -- and turns instead to Justice Secretary Menardo Guevarra, who has the authority to discipline the erring policemen and prosecutors and to pursue motion for reconsideration in the RTC or certiorari in the CA or SC. The civic stakes, he warns, are larger than this case: unless justice is restored, citizens may turn to 'authoritarian shortcuts' and 'shoot first and ask questions later' mercenaries.
